title: Lesson 33: Measuring adoption over quarters, not weeks
description: Grounded in Lesson 33 of the AI Adoption series: measurement windows and reachable denominators, the habit threshold, cohort retention curves, why weekly cadence produces false signals, the three steering-agenda numbers, telling saturation from a stall, and the six-check sequence for separating calendar noise and metric defects from a real decline.

questions.question: A program's habitual use rate has held between 38 and 41 percent for three quarters. Fanned out, cohort curves show the February group reached 54 percent and flattened, May reached 47, and the August cohort reached 39 percent and was still climbing at quarter end. Based on Lesson 33, what does that pattern indicate?
options: Saturation, because the aggregate has stopped rising, so the program should stop buying seats and shift to depth
A stall, because later cohorts are performing worse than earlier ones, so the enablement program should be rebuilt from scratch
A measurement defect, because cohort curves cannot differ from the aggregate if the same definition is used

Later cohorts improving while starting lower, which points to an enablement and workflow-fit problem rather than saturation, since a saturation plateau would show curves converging on a similar asymptote
questions.explanation: Lesson 33 distinguishes three causes of a flat aggregate. Converging curves that reach a similar asymptote indicate saturation. Curves that start at the same height and descend faster in later waves indicate enablement debt. Curves that flatten lower than earlier ones but are still climbing indicate exactly what the August cohort shows: later cohorts have harder jobs or worse onboarding, which is a scoping and enablement fact. The worked example traces the gap to a kickoff cut from 90 minutes to 20, and answers with a rebuilt day-one session rather than more licenses.

questions.question: In Q4 an organization sees habitual use rate fall from 41 to 38 percent, returning rate fall from 72 to 64 percent, and depth fall from 6.0 to 5.2 actions per active user. What does Lesson 33 say the order of investigation should be?
options: Start with a strategy review of the AI roadmap, since three metrics moving together is a program failure signal

Start with the cheap and common explanations in order: composition of the base, window and delay, instrument and definition changes, calendar effects, then run chart and control chart rules, stopping at the first check that explains the movement
Start with control chart limits, because statistical rules must confirm the decline before any business explanation is considered
Start with a user survey, because only users can explain why usage changed
questions.explanation: Lesson 33 gives a fixed six-check sequence in that order because the cheap explanations are also the most common, and a program that opens with a strategy debate about a data defect wastes a quarter of goodwill. The worked example runs the same sequence: a reorganisation moved 60 people out of the reachable population, December holiday weeks repeated a known seasonal dip, and two metrics had been redefined or were being read from a dashboard with a different window. Two of the four metrics in that example were instrument problems, which is why arithmetic gets ruled out before behavior.

questions.question: An operator plots weekly active users on a run chart with the median as the centre line and sees seven consecutive weekly points below the median, with no single point far outside the pattern. Based on Lesson 33, how should that be read?
options: As noise, because no point broke the three sigma limit and only extreme points count
As a shift, because six or more consecutive points on one side of the median is the run chart rule for a shift, which means the movement deserves investigation even without an extreme point
As proof that the program declined, because any run of points below the median is a confirmed decline
As a trend, because a trend is defined as five or more consecutive points moving in one direction
questions.explanation: Lesson 33 cites the run chart rules: a shift is six or more consecutive points above or below the median, a trend is five or more consecutive points all increasing or decreasing, and an astronomical point is one so far outside the pattern that it needs a specific explanation. Seven points below the median therefore meets the shift rule, which is a signal to look rather than a conclusion. The lesson also pairs that with its decision rule: a single quarter with a movement gets a note, and two consecutive quarters with a sustained shift plus a nameable mechanism gets a decision.
